summary: Summation No. 17 covers February 1947, a month dominated by Japanese politics and economic strain. General MacArthur's 20 February message to Congress defended occupation appropriations and food relief, and on 6 February he urged Prime Minister Yoshida to hold a new general election, which the Government scheduled for 5-30 April ahead of the new Constitution taking effect on 3 May. The report details failed coalition talks with the Social Democrats, Liberal-Progressive merger manoeuvres, labor politics after the cancelled 1 February general strike, and the 92nd Diet reconvening on 14 February. Economic sections give January figures showing coal, power and raw-material shortages depressing production, a 20 February plan to raise government wages to an average of 1,200 yen, rising inflation, the capital levy and a 10 billion yen supplemental budget. Social sections cover repatriation, relief, disease statistics, school reform and war crimes trials, including the opening of the defense case before the International Military Tribunal. Dense statistical tables and charts make it a useful reference for historians.
highlights: On 20 February MacArthur sent Congress a message arguing that victory required a Japanese 'spiritual reformation' and that appropriated relief food was not charity, citing Bataan and the cost of starvation and unrest.

On 6 February MacArthur urged Prime Minister Yoshida to hold a new general election; the Government set 5 April for executives, 20 April for the House of Councillors, 25 April for the House of Representatives, 30 April for local assemblies.

Four coalition attempts involving the Social Democrats failed, their Central Executive Committee refusing on 14 February; Shidehara proposed a Liberal-Progressive merger on 19 February amid six Liberal and four Progressive factions.
After the 1 February general strike was called off, government wages were to rise to an average of 1,200 yen a month (announced 20 February); union membership stood at 4,415,482 in 17,163 unions.

January coal output was 2,009,400 metric tons, with a Government five-point plan aimed at a 30,000,000-ton 1947-48 goal; power generation rose 1.7 percent to 2,518,000,000 kWh but shortages stayed severe.
A train overturned near Hachioji on 25 February, killing 178 and injuring about 800; Bank of Japan notes in circulation reached 105,489,919,000 yen and capital levy collection began 15 February.

Twelve war crimes trials with 32 defendants finished in Japan with eight death sentences, 977 suspects were held in Sugamo, and the defense opened its case before the International Military Tribunal on 25 February.
Repatriation brought 95,644 Japanese home from 27 January to the end of February, with 1,273,278 still awaiting return from Soviet-controlled areas; January births totaled 275,221 and deaths 117,489.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Cover for Summation No. 17 (February 1947), table of contents for Parts I-IV, and the list of 106 charts, maps and graphs.

sections.title: Part I: General
sections.summary: Monthly digest: no SCAP reorganization, MacArthur's 20 February message to Congress and 6 February election letter, January economic indicators, and social items on relief, repatriation and education.

sections.title: Section 1. Organization Under SCAP
sections.summary: No change occurred in the non-military organization of General Headquarters, SCAP, during February.

sections.title: Section 2. Political Activities
sections.summary: MacArthur's 20 February message to Congress and 6 February election letter, the reorganized Yoshida Cabinet, the reconvened Diet, the Hachioji train wreck and war crimes trials.

sections.title: Section 3. Economic Activities
sections.summary: January indicators: coal and steel gains, but power shortages cut chemicals to 30 percent of minimum needs; textiles declined; 1,200-yen government wage plan, 105 billion yen in notes, 10 billion yen budget.

sections.title: Section 4. Social Activities
sections.summary: Relief to 2,891,336 persons, 95,644 repatriated, new Education Minister, women admitted to higher schools, Shinto directives, popular radio programs and record SCAP library attendance.

sections.title: Part II: Political
sections.summary: Government and party politics around the Yoshida Cabinet and elections, public safety statistics, Japanese courts, and war crimes prosecutions including the opening of the defense at the Tokyo Tribunal.

sections.title: Section 1. Government and Politics
sections.summary: MacArthur's Congress message with press comment, local government reform, failed coalition and merger moves, inflation, labor politics, the 92nd Diet and the April 1947 election schedule.

sections.title: Supreme Commander's Message to Congress
sections.summary: Full text of MacArthur's message urging 'complete spiritual reformation' and relief funds, plus Nihon Keizai, Mainichi and Asahi editorials of 26-27 February.

sections.title: Local Government Reform
sections.summary: Thirteen planned changes under the new Constitution: popularly responsible governors, assembly powers over budgets and appointments, initiative, referendum and recall, and nonpartisan election committees.

sections.title: Political Developments
sections.summary: Cool reception of the revised Cabinet, four failed coalition proposals, six Liberal and four Progressive factions, merger plans, and the Japan Farmers' Party formed 21 February.

sections.title: Inflation and Politics
sections.summary: Social Democrats' eight-point anti-inflation program of 5 February rejected 'Ishibashi inflation' and was adopted by both wings of the party.

sections.title: Labor and Politics
sections.summary: Prewar labor parties, Matsuoka's re-election as head of the General Federation of Trade Unions, the NCIU, Social Democrats, Communists, and the Farmers' Union split of 12 February.

sections.title: The Diet
sections.summary: The 92nd Diet reconvened 14 February with Liberals holding 148 seats; Tokyo papers called Yoshida's opening speech on coal, controls and labor 'abstract'.

sections.title: General Elections
sections.summary: MacArthur's 6 February letter, party and union responses, the 17 February schedule of elections from 5 to 30 April, and Asahi and Yomiuri comment.

sections.title: Section 2. Public Safety
sections.summary: Osaka black-market raids led to 5,215 arrests; 135,909 offenses in December; Hachioji train wreck killed 178; also radio patrol cars, juvenile delinquency, prison surveys and fires.

sections.title: Section 3. Legal and War Crimes
sections.summary: Judicial appointments of 7 February, occupation courts, 977 suspects in Sugamo, trials in Japan and the Philippines, and the Tokyo Tribunal defense's opening statement of 25-26 February.

sections.title: Legal Affairs and Japanese Judicial Administration
sections.summary: Chinese representatives in provost courts; on 7 February Hosono became Supreme Court President, Tanimura Vice-minister of Justice and Kimura Prosecutor-general.

sections.title: Military Occupation Courts
sections.summary: Thefts of U.S. goods, impersonation of Occupation personnel and aiding deserters were tried; Eighth Army courts handled 1,137 cases from 21 December to 20 January.

sections.title: Investigation, Apprehension and Prosecution of War Criminals
sections.summary: Eight apprehension memorandums, 977 held in Sugamo, 571 Japanese held in the Philippines, 148 defendants tried in Japan to date, and British trials with 30 death sentences.

sections.title: International Prosecution of War Criminals
sections.summary: Tribunal denied dismissal motions on 3 February and reconvened 24 February; the defense opening covered Manchuria, China, the USSR and the Pacific War, arguing self-defense.

sections.title: Part III: Economic
sections.summary: January production, trade, labor, price and finance data: coal, power and material shortages limited industry, while trade, rationing, the capital levy and property control advanced.

sections.title: Section 1. Agriculture and Fisheries
sections.summary: 1946 crop review citing fertilizer shortage (75,400 of 380,000 tons nitrate), land commissions, soil survey, January fish landings of 88,608 tons, and whaling and fishing fuel controls.

sections.title: Section 2. Forestry and Mining
sections.summary: January logs at 453,040,000 board feet, coal output 2,009,400 tons with a five-point plan for a 30,000,000-ton goal, lignite shortfall, oil drilling and mineral production.

sections.title: Forestry
sections.summary: Log production rose 21,240,000 board feet to 453,040,000; stockpiles reached 1,610,120,000 board feet; 19,339 sawmills operated; firewood and charcoal figures.

sections.title: Mining
sections.summary: Coal, lignite, coal consumption by industry, petroleum drilling, and December mineral and metal output, with antimony the only significant gain.

sections.title: Section 3. Heavy Industries
sections.summary: Coke 104,500 tons, aluminum 1,024 tons, cement 73,954 tons; chemical output at 30 percent of minimum needs, machinery down 25 percent, housing starts and textile machinery gains.

sections.title: Section 4. Manufacturing
sections.summary: Food processing, pulp and paper, glass, ceramics, electrical goods, vehicles, 767 tons of crude rubber, leather and farm tools, mostly curtailed by power shortages.

sections.title: Section 5. Textile Industries
sections.summary: Yarn output fell with holidays and power limits; mills received 34,332,000 pounds of cotton, 818,614 bales shipped, silk fabrics down to 1,458,000 square yards, rayon staple 684,000 pounds.

sections.title: Section 6. Transportation and Public Utilities
sections.summary: Motor vehicles up to 115,587, rail freight down 417,200 tons, power generation 2,518,000,000 kWh (up 1.7 percent) with coal deliveries 66 percent short, gas at 23 percent of capacity.

sections.title: Section 7. Communications
sections.summary: Telephones up one percent, 123,000 new radio licenses, postal money orders up 43 percent, Kyoto and Kobe exchange rehabilitation, and the 19 February freeze of International Telecommunications Company assets.

sections.title: Section 8. Labor
sections.summary: Union membership 4,415,482, Coal Industry Reconstruction Council of 5 February, 2,000 collective agreements, strike statistics, 20 February wage rise plan and employment programs.

sections.title: Labor Legislation and Organizations
sections.summary: Labor Standards and other bills before the Diet, union statistics, the Economic Reconstruction Council, federation politics and the Kanto Employers' Association's principles.

sections.title: Labor Relations
sections.summary: Tokyo Labor Relations Committee elections of 12 February, tax collectors' agreement of 6 February, 101 disputes in December, and the Supreme Court ruling in the Toyo Watch case.

sections.title: Labor Education, Wages and Employment
sections.summary: Tokyo Imperial University labor lectures, price rises eroding wages, government wage raise to 1,200 yen, railway hours agreement, labor census, 1,991 handicraft centers and coal-mine schools.

sections.title: Section 9. Imports and Exports
sections.summary: January trade: tea, silk goods and bamboo to the United States, textile machinery and chemicals to Korea, wheat, cotton and sugar imports, plus a 1946 review covering 10 countries.

sections.title: Section 10. Rationing and Price Control
sections.summary: Staple food collections of 3,264,000 tons, 87,500 tons of imported food released, vegetable subsidy ended, fuel gas and tram fares raised, 48 critical items rationed.

sections.title: Section 11. Finance
sections.summary: Notes in circulation 105,489,919,000 yen, capital levy from 15 February, 10 billion yen bond issue, national debt of 263,855,000,000 yen, and foreign exchange surrender extended to 31 January.

sections.title: Section 12. Property Control and Reparations
sections.summary: Looted property valued at 6,397,012 yen in storage, approved loans to textile and steel firms, holding company liquidation and reparations delegations in Japan.

sections.title: Property Control
sections.summary: German properties, looted goods, firms in liquidation, dissolved organizations, precious metals, the SCAP yen custody account, four new claims and releases from custody.

sections.title: Antitrust, Cartels and Reparations
sections.summary: Credit approvals including 3,133,170,000 yen for 17 fertilizer firms, Holding Company Liquidation Commission instructions of 16 January, and reparations delegations from Australia, China and the Netherlands.

sections.title: Part IV: Social
sections.summary: Public health, welfare, veterinary and disease statistics, then education, religion, information programs, press and media, ending with a map of Japan.

sections.title: Section 1. Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: Relief to 2,891,336 persons, 95,644 repatriated, Red Cross budget, meat and milk inspection, penicillin supply, narcotics, communicable disease and January vital statistics.

sections.title: Welfare and Repatriation
sections.summary: Relief payments of 160,232,312 yen, repatriate reception centers, Japanese Red Cross proposed budget, social security and hospital administration.

sections.title: Veterinary, Dental and Nursing Affairs
sections.summary: Meat and milk inspection figures, animal disease reports, rehabilitation of bombed-out dentists and the public health nurses' course.

sections.title: Supply
sections.summary: Simplified penicillin extraction, medical and dental supply production, biologicals, distribution list cut from 201 to 124 items, and narcotics controls.

sections.title: Preventive Medicine and Vital Statistics
sections.summary: Dysentery, typhoid, smallpox, typhus, malaria and cholera reports, communicable diseases by prefecture, and January births of 275,221 and deaths of 117,489.

sections.title: Section 2. Education, Religion and Media of Expression
sections.summary: New Education Minister Takahashi, women admitted to higher schools, Shinto directives, election and women's information programs, radio, press comment, film attendance of 804,375 and library records.

sections.title: Education, Religion and Arts
sections.summary: New higher-school entrance plan, Parent-Teacher Association pamphlet, 6-3-3-4 school handbook, Shinto separation rules, missionaries and inventories of private art collections.

sections.title: Media of Expression
sections.summary: Information programs on women, health, labor and the Constitution, radio shows, press comment, kabuki, educational films and 639 daily library visitors.
